segments.summary: Older than classmates, he passed into the main orchestra, heard Copland's 'El Salon Mexico' and decided to become a composer.

segments.title: Arguing with Peter Mennin about jazz at Juilliard
segments.summary: He challenged composition teacher Peter Mennin on Juilliard ignoring jazz, won the class with J.J. Johnson's sound, and credits Wynton Marsalis for later change.

segments.title: Ending the first session and starting the second
segments.summary: They check on his health, agree to stop and plan the next session for after Juilliard. The second day opens December 11.

segments.title: Truman's band becomes a conservatory at Dachau
segments.summary: Truman had the barracks turned into a conservatory. General Huebner enlarged the band to 82 and Frankfurt Symphony teachers were paid in cigarettes, chocolate and stockings.

segments.title: Desegregation of the armed forces began with the band
segments.summary: He argues the band showed Black musicians' capability, proved a model, and that Truman then outlawed segregation without using the word.

segments.title: Mrs. Campbell, Frita Jones and the 'Estrellita' trombonist
segments.summary: He regrets losing touch with Mrs. Campbell and Jeanie, then recounts hearing 'Estrellita' sung by Frita Jones and played in the Army dance band.

segments.title: Meeting Ernest Outlaw
segments.summary: He describes Outlaw, a Chicago clarinetist and saxophonist who played on German radio, taught him Ellington and Parker, and taught him to play as if life depended on it.

segments.title: Outlaw's Cicero story and Freddie Williams
segments.summary: Outlaw's funny story of being stopped by Cicero police after a lesson, and how Outlaw steered him toward the true player at a jam session.

segments.title: Teaching himself trombone and embouchure
segments.summary: He was self-taught on trombone except for a Frankfurt teacher, and explains how smiling on the mouthpiece ruined his embouchure, which should be a pucker anchored at the jaw.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Trombone lessons at Juilliard
segments.summary: A Met Opera first-chair teacher told him to choose between money and learning the trombone, and said they would work on what comes out of the horn. He developed a classical sound.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Leaving the Army for Juilliard on the G.I. Bill
segments.summary: He planned a safe 20 years of Army service as a master sergeant, then chose Juilliard instead of being a big fish in a little pond.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Last lesson with Roger Smith
segments.summary: His teacher Roger Smith asked him to play one middle B flat to show everything he had learned: sound, personality and pulse.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Joining Charles Mingus's tentet at the Five Spot
segments.summary: Mingus gave each player a single note on paper and no score. The band opened that night, and Mingus announced McIntosh's piece 'Malice Toward None'.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Mingus arrives late and the near fight
segments.summary: Mingus came in late, shouted about toilet paper, and accused McIntosh of trying to take over when he played piano. McIntosh stood ready to defend himself.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Black students and jazz at Juilliard; the jam sessions
segments.summary: Frank Perowsky and he taught each other jazz at jam sessions at Count Basie's club, hearing Cannonball Adderley and Freddie Hubbard arrive.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Tommy Flanagan, Dizzy Gillespie and getting known
segments.summary: Jimmy Minger sent him to Tommy Flanagan, who recorded his pieces; Dizzy Gillespie then called him a favorite composer and arranger and taught him not to care about race.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: James Moody in Germany and at the Port Authority
segments.summary: He met Moody at a Jazz at the Philharmonic date in Germany, and years later gave Moody his last dollars at the Port Authority while his wife-to-be called Moody a bum.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Tape break
segments.summary: Recording stops for a break.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Quincy Jones's rise
segments.summary: He tells how Quincy Jones came to Dizzy, Lionel Hampton and Liberty Records, Lena Horne's show in Europe, and compares Truman's and Eisenhower's use of Black artists.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Lucky Thompson, Paramount hire and Lee Stevens
segments.summary: He recalls Quincy turning Lucky Thompson away, then being hired at Paramount as the first Black staff composer under Lee Stevens, who died suddenly.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Quincy calls him uncommercial
segments.summary: Quincy told people Mac was a great composer but the most uncommercial one he knew, and McIntosh agrees, saying he wrote for Miles, Dizzy and Coltrane.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Jamming at John Coltrane's place
segments.summary: Flanagan took him to jam with Coltrane, who gave them one hour of his time and praised McIntosh's chorus on 'Like Someone in Love'.

segments.chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
segments.title: Coltrane's Bible talk and Thad Jones's recording of his chart
segments.summary: He told Coltrane about love, wisdom, justice and power, then wrote 'balanced scales' for the Thad Jones band, which Brookmeyer insisted be recorded in one take.

segments.title: Joining the Jazztet
segments.summary: Benny Golson and Art Farmer overheard him practicing in Washington and, after Curtis Fuller left, asked him to audition.

segments.title: Dinah Washington pay and Hines on the bible
segments.summary: Dinah Washington propositioned him when he came for pay and he refused as a new Witness. Then at the Apollo the Hines father threw his Bible in the trash.

segments.title: The Bible in the trash and Jehovah's Witnesses
segments.summary: He confronted the elder Hines, citing scripture, and Kenny Dorham backed him up. Dinah Washington later blamed him for taking Christmas from children.

segments.title: Bible classes and trouble at Paramount
segments.summary: As Lee Stevens' assistant he was promoted, but after Stevens died the new boss objected to his lunch hour Bible study and looked for ways to fire him.

segments.title: The Monk program at New England Conservatory
segments.summary: At the New England Conservatory he directed the Monk program, found the role was ceremonial, and again ran into his religion. He praises Helen Sung.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: Bags Jackson, Moody's band and the Hip String Quartet
segments.summary: He explains arranging for Moody, learning audience building from the MJQ and John Lewis, and writing the Hip String Quartet album for Milt Jackson, later a brass version.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: Gordon Parks introduced; break
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about Gordon Parks, McIntosh starts on John Cassavetes, and recording stops.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: The soldier who painted himself to live in Africa
segments.summary: A funny tale of a soldier who darkened his skin with shoe polish to desert and live in Africa, and was caught because he swatted flies.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: Soviet agents targeting the Army band
segments.summary: He says Soviet agents targeted complaining members of Truman's band for Radio Moscow, and that he blends fact and imagination in his film story.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: Willie Cox and the Cadillac
segments.summary: Willie Cox asked Soviet agents what car Stalin drove and, hearing no Cadillac, left them with nothing to offer.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: Gordon Parks, Henry Brant and the call to score The Learning Tree
segments.summary: Parks's plan for a first Black film auteur led him to Henry Brant, who recommended Golson and McIntosh. Golson declined and McIntosh got the job.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: Writing the score and the Dizzy rhythm lesson
segments.summary: Stuck on an hour of continuous music, he asked basic questions and recalled Dizzy saying he looks for the next rhythm. He then finished the score.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: Parks takes the main title credit
segments.summary: Academy members offered a nomination if McIntosh was credited, but Gordon Parks refused, a betrayal that Parks's secretary also saw.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: Shaft and Isaac Hayes
segments.summary: He was brought in to supervise Isaac Hayes on Shaft because Hayes could not write music, and learned how Hayes's music was heard at the Academy Awards.

segments.chapter: Bags Jackson, Army tales and Gordon Parks films
segments.title: Isaac Hayes's deal and the sequel
segments.summary: Hayes avoided signing a buyout and gained leverage, and McIntosh helped on the sequel against his agent's advice out of loyalty to Parks.

segments.title: What film scoring teaches: emotion and rhythm
segments.summary: Jazz musicians think sound, film composers think emotion, and universities never teach rhythm. He relates this to Miles Davis focusing on feeling.

segments.title: The MTV idea and the sea piece
segments.summary: He suggests using music to pre-sell video, then describes his sea-inspired piece and what listeners wanted from it.

segments.title: 'All Blues' and The Gandy Dancers
segments.summary: He says Miles Davis cited a spiritual for 'All Blues', and pitches a film about the Gandy Dancers.

segments.title: Music today and the history of music as Adam and Eve
segments.summary: Asked about music today, he argues the history of music is young men celebrating women, from Adam to The Beatles.

segments.title: Blues, minstrelsy and the Jubilee
segments.summary: The talk turns to blues versus European art, minstrel shows as mockery, and his view that liberty and Jubilee in Leviticus shaped slavery and black music.

segments.title: Roy Haynes and Kenny Clarke on drumming as conversation
segments.summary: Good drummers extend what others play. He recalls Kenny Clarke making his early playing sound like music.

segments.title: Thinking like a drummer: J.J. Johnson and rhythmic surprise
segments.summary: J.J. Johnson played like a drummer, placing notes before, on or after the beat, which keeps the ear guessing.

segments.title: Directing Moody's group and the bass problem
segments.summary: Moody made him director, and he persuaded Moody to replace the bassist with Ernest Outlaw.

segments.title: Recruiting Outlaw and Pat Patrick; Moody repays the dollar
segments.summary: He recruited Outlaw in Chicago, who brought Pat Patrick on baritone. Moody later returned clean and repaid the dollar to McIntosh's wife.

segments.title: Pat Patrick's illness and his father
segments.summary: He recalls Pat Patrick, dying of cancer, thanking him for the Moody job, and wishes to speak to Patrick's father.

segments.title: Closing thanks and the Bush letter
segments.summary: Kimery thanks him for two days; McIntosh hopes his story will be told and mentions a letter from President George W. Bush.
